description: Somos Coffee Devs de La Paz listo para meterle código y datos al reto Field Shift. Queremos transformar observaciones satelitales de la NASA en alertas y recomendaciones reales para el campo boliviano. Si sabes de datos, agronomía, IA o sabes contar buenas historias para el pitch, súmate.
summary:
Yanapiri, which means “the one who helps” in Aymara and Quechua, is a free agronomic copilot that helps small farmers in Bolivia decide what to plant before they invest. Farmers mark their community on a map, choose their current crop, set a priority (earn more, save water, or protect the soil), and describe their real situation, such as “I have few irrigation turns.” Yanapiri then compares three crop rotation options side by side, shows what happens if the same crop is repeated, and explains in everyday language what is gained and sacrificed in each alternative. A drought simulator shows how each option holds up under stress.
It is designed for family farmers and municipalities in Bolivia, starting in La Paz. Nearly 40 municipalities in the department are in a climate emergency (22 from drought and 18 from flooding), and over 100,000 Bolivian families are losing harvests to El Niño. More than 80% of small farmers depend on rainfall alone and have no weather station on their land, while aid arrives only after the disaster.
Yanapiri turns NASA satellite data into simple, local guidance, with no sensors and no cost to the farmer. It shifts the response from reacting to emergencies to preventing them. Results are indicative and should be validated with local knowledge and field observation..
details:
What it does and how it works

Yanapiri is an agronomic copilot for farm plot planning. Users select their location, draw their plot on an interactive 3D map, choose their current crop from the INE Bolivia catalog, and define a priority (higher income, water savings, or soil care). They can optionally describe their real situation in free text. The system queries temperature, frost risk, rainfall, wind, and root-zone moisture, and combines them with soil estimates and local crop data to calculate how viable each option is. The result is a visual comparison of three rotation alternatives, with risks, environmental conditions, and care recommendations. A scenario simulator (drought, heavy rain, heat, or frost) shows how each alternative responds. These scenarios are indicative and are not forecasts.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Reduces investment risk for farmers by letting them decide with data instead of blindly.
  • It is free and requires no sensors or weather stations on the farm.
  • Translates complex environmental data into explanations that are easy to understand.
  • Allows municipalities and cooperatives to do preventive planning at a minimal cost compared with responding to emergencies.

Target audience and rationale

The target audience is small farmers and municipalities in Bolivia, with initial validation in La Paz. This group was chosen because of the scale of the current problem:

  • Nearly 40 municipalities in La Paz are in a climate emergency as of November 2026: 22 due to drought and 18 due to flooding.
  • Over 100,000 Bolivian families are losing harvests to El Niño.
  • More than 80% of small farmers depend only on rainfall (INE Bolivia).
  • Climate variability and slope erosion can reduce yields by up to 35% (IPCC).
  • Millions of bolivianos are spent responding to disasters after they happen, rather than preventing them.

NASA data used

  • NASA POWER: daily, monthly, and historical climatology variables, queried by point or polygon, at the 10 to 15 km scale that matches the resolution of the satellite data.
  • Soil estimates to assess root-zone moisture and erosion.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Cesium (3D map and scenario exploration).
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI, using a layered architecture (controllers, services, schemas, core, ml). It integrates NASA POWER and soil estimates.
  • AI: Gemini generates explanations and recommendations based on the calculated data.
  • Local data: the INE Bolivia crop catalog and moisture and temperature requirements per crop (potato, fava bean, corn, oat).

Creativity and factors considered

  • Compares rotations side by side instead of using technical charts, and shows the cost of repeating the same crop.
  • Incorporates the farmer’s real situation, such as limited irrigation turns.
  • Explanations are given in everyday language with a local focus.
  • Results are treated as indicative and should be cross-checked with local knowledge and field observations.
  • Next steps: offline mode and expansion across Bolivia.

Links

  • Code repository: https://github.com/ijquenta/coffeedevs-fieldshift-nasa
  • Deployed backend: https://yanapiri-backend-production.up.railway.app/docs
  • Deployed frontend: https://coffeedevs-fieldshift-nasa-front.vercel.app/
